title: Metallic electron crystals in rhombohedral graphene as a bridge to twisted WSe$_2$
authors: Wentai Deng, Chenyuan Li, Naoto Nakatsuji, Fang Xie, Lei Chen, Qimiao Si, Jennifer Cano
abstract: Superconducting phases have recently been discovered both in twisted bilayers of transition metal dichalcogenide WSe$_2$ (tWSe$_2$) and in rhombohedral multilayer graphene (RMG). While both have generated extensive interest, they appear to be driven by qualitatively different physics. Here, we propose a unified picture in which the superconductivity in RMG arises from a strongly correlated metallic state with a spatial length scale that is compatible with the moiré length scale of tWSe$_2$. Central to this mechanism is a Wigner crystal phase in RMG that is metallic, driven by a "W"-shaped dispersion in the flat part of the underlying graphene band structure. We demonstrate this effect through calculations of Wigner crystal states in pentalayer RMG, focusing on dilute electrons in the quarter-metal regime relevant to experiment. In a region of the phase diagram we find the Wigner crystal breaks three-fold rotation symmetry, which guides our construction of a $t$-$V$ model on a triangular lattice as an effective description of the low-energy electronic physics. This construction suggests a surprisingly similar low-energy description of RMG and tWSe$_2$. Broader implications for superconductivity in dilute carrier systems are also discussed.
summary: This work unifies the understanding of superconductivity in rhombohedral graphene and twisted WSe2 by proposing that both systems are governed by a metallic Wigner crystal phase. Through advanced HF calculations, the authors derive an effective t-V model that captures the low-energy electronic structure, suggesting a common underlying physics for superconductivity in these correlated 2D materials.
main_problem: To propose a unified physical picture connecting the superconductivity observed in rhombohedral multilayer graphene (RMG) and twisted bilayer WSe2.
main_result: The superconductivity in RMG is linked to a metallic Wigner crystal phase, which shares a surprisingly similar low-energy description (a t-V model) with that of tWSe2.
method: The study employs self-consistent Hartree-Fock (HF) calculations on continuum and lattice models, followed by constructing and analyzing an effective t-V Hamiltonian.
model_or_system: The primary system is rhombohedral multilayer graphene (RMG), modeled with an interlayer potential. The low-energy physics is captured by an effective t-V model on a triangular lattice, mirroring the physics of twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides.
key_observables: Crystalline order parameter $|ho(\mathbf{G})|$, Chern number ($C$), band structure, and the effective Hamiltonian parameters.
important_parameters: Electron concentration ($n$), interlayer potential ($\delta D$), and the moiré length scale inherent to the twisted bilayer systems.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the Hartree-Fock approximation and assumes the existence of a metallic Wigner crystal phase that dictates the low-energy physics.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the phase diagram showing transitions between insulating and metallic Wigner crystal states, the resulting band structures, and the symmetry breaking associated with the metallic phase.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the correlated metallic state in RMG via HF calculations, identifying the symmetry breaking, and then deriving a minimal effective t-V model whose low-energy physics is compared directly to that of tWSe2.
why_interesting: The concept of emergent, correlated electronic phases (like metallic Wigner crystals) providing a universal low-energy description across different physical platforms (graphene vs. TMDs) is highly relevant to understanding unconventional superconductivity in strongly correlated systems.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. (a) Phase diagram for Wigner crystallization as a function of the electron density n and interlayer potential δD. |ρ(G)| is the order parameter quantifying the broken continuous translation symmetry. The red and black dashed lines respectively mark the onset of the crystalline phase (|ρ(G)| > 0.02) and the metal-to-insulator transition. (b-c) The first conduction band of the noninteracting R5G band structure. The dispersion becomes “W”-shaped for sufficiently large displacement field potential δD, leading to multiple Fermi surfaces. (d-e) Line cuts of |ρ(G)| vs. n for two fixed interlayer potentials.

FIG. 2. Insulating WC states. (a-b) The band structure and real space density distribution of the HF solution at δD = −25 meV and n = 0.3 × 1012 cm−2. (c-d) Same plots but at δD = −30 meV and n = 0.8×1012 cm−2. Red curves indicate the top valence band with Chern number C indicated.

FIG. 3. Metallic WC state. (a) HF band structure at δD = −40 meV and n = 0.8×1012 cm−2. The two conduction bands near the Fermi level, denoted CB1 and CB2, are highlighted by red curves. (b) Real space density distribution. (c-d) Dispersion of the first and second conduction bands (CB1 and CB2). The black solid line shows the Brillouin zone of this crystalline state, and the dashed curves show the Fermi surfaces, consisting of a hole and an electron pocket around the γ and k′ points, respectively.

FIG. 5. Effective t-V model. (a) Schematic of the hon- eycomb lattice with A orbitals at the 1b Wyckoff position (red dots) and B orbitals at the 1c Wyckoff position (blue squares). Marker sizes reflects the local real space density for each orbital. Dotted lines mark the unit cell of the underlying triangular Bravais lattice, while dashed lines denote density- density interaction bonds. (b) Non-interacting band structure of the effective model, parametrized to reproduce the princi- pal features of the two relevant HF bands at δD = −40 meV and n = 0.8 × 1012cm−2. Red and blue indicate the A- and B-orbital weights. (c, d) Momentum distribution n(k) for VA = VB = 3 meV and VA = VB = 30 meV,...

FIG. 4. Metallic WC state with C3z-symmetry breaking. The model parameters are δD = −45 meV and n = 1.1×1012 cm−2. (a) HF band structure. (b) Real space density distribution. (c-d) Dispersion of the first and second conduction bands (CB1 and CB2). The dashed curves show the Fermi surfaces, consisting of a hole pocket around γ and an electron pocket that encloses a k-m-k′ segment.
